title: Snap a magnet in half
hook: One end of a bar magnet is north, the other south. Break it: what does each half get?

knows: magnets have a north and a south end
doesNotKnow: that a magnet is made of countless tiny atomic magnets lined up, so every piece, however small, has both poles; there is no lone north pole

misconception: Snapping a bar magnet in half separates its north pole from its south pole.
objective: The learner can explain that every piece of a magnet has both a north and a south pole, because a magnet is built from tiny atomic magnets lined up head to tail.

claims.text: Every piece of a magnet, however small, has both a north and a south pole; magnetic field lines have no start or end (stage: N and S letters on every piece's faces, 'every piece: N + S'; reveal: 'any piece has a north end and a south end').
claims.source: Gauss's law for magnetism, ∇·B = 0: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, chapter 5 (magnetostatics). Brief claim 1.

claims.text: A bar magnet's magnetism comes from countless tiny atomic magnets (atomic magnetic moments, grouped in domains) lined up head to tail (stage: the arrows inside the bar, caption 'Arrows are the tiny atomic magnets'; reveal: 'A magnet is built from countless tiny atomic magnets lined up head to tail').
claims.source: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, chapter 6 (magnetic fields in matter; ferromagnetism and domains). Brief claim 2.

claims.text: Snapped in the middle, the break shows a new south pole on the north half and a new north pole on the other half, and the halves attract; with one half turned round the facing poles are S and S and the halves push apart (stage: compasses at the break, labels 'S | N at the break: they pull together', 'S | S: they push apart'; Seen row; reveal first paragraph).
claims.source: Coaxial point-dipole chain force sum for two 5-unit halves with a 0.1 gap: attractive as cut, repulsive with one half reversed (artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs, block 'snap-the-magnet'). In the pole model each piece carries +σA on its N face and −σA on its S face (net 0). Brief claim 3.

claims.text: Nobody has ever found a lone north pole (an isolated magnetic monopole) (reveal).
claims.source: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, chapter 5 (no magnetic monopoles have been found); Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics, magnetic monopole searches. Brief claim 4.

claims.text: Compass convention: the compass's filled (north) end points away from an N face and towards an S face, along the field on the bar's axis; beside the middle of the whole bar the field runs from the N end towards the S end and there is no pole (stage: 'Compass: the filled end is its north end.', 'middle: no pole').
claims.source: Field outside a magnet runs from N to S; a compass needle's north end points along the field (any introductory text, e.g. Griffiths chapter 5). Demo.tsx Compass.

claims.text: Idealisations: a uniformly magnetised bar, a clean break, and no loss of magnetism from the snap. The arrows are a picture of the alignment, not a count of atoms.

recall.question: You cut a fridge magnet into ten strips. How many of the strips have a north pole?
recall.why: Each strip is still made of tiny atomic magnets lined up, so each has its own north and south pole.
